claims.text: Benandanti of Friuli, born with the caul, spirits left bodies on Ember Days to fight witches with fennel vs sorghum stalks; Gasparutto and Moduco questioned by a priest 1575, case reopened 1580 by Felice da Montefalco, admitted deceived by Devil, sentenced 1581 to six months, remitted; Inquisition came to regard them as witches, testimony reshaped toward diabolical sabbath; no case concluded 1575–1619; Ginzburg 1966, English 1983; fertility-cult thesis criticised by Cohn ('nothing whatsoever') and Hutton

Domenico Scandella, b. 1532, miller of Montereale Valcellina, Republic of Venice; read works on religion and history; tried 1583, abjured 1584, ~20 months prison, released 1586; arrested 1598 as lapsed heretic, declared heresiarch 1599, burned 1599; Ginzburg, The Cheese and the Worms, 1976

Practitioners of folk magic medieval to early 20th c.: countering witchcraft, finding stolen property and missing persons, fortune-telling, healing people and livestock, love magic; poorer people could not afford physicians; Davies: 'as many as several thousand' in England; 1541 Act targeted witches and cunning folk, repealed by 1547; 1563 Act milder; 1735 Act treated claims as fraud; Vagrancy Act 1824; rarely accused: Essex ~400 tried, 4 identifiable cunning folk; Catholic, Anglican, Protestant authorities saw them as in league with the Devil, Quakers vocal; vanished by 1940s
